videos.title: From Wet Lab to RL Env: 10,000 Drug-Discovery Campaigns in a Weekend — Ian Quigley, Leash Bio
videos.description:
From a four-billion-measurement Kaggle competition to models that recognize a molecule’s chemist, Leash Bio is testing what AI actually learns about chemistry. Co-founder and CEO Ian Quigley joins Brandon Anderson and RJ Honicky to explain how Leash makes DNA-encoded libraries (DELs) produce clean, reproducible protein–small-molecule binding data—and why collecting the right experiments matters as much as choosing a model.

We go deep on hidden shortcuts in public datasets, Hermes’ comparison with Boltz, and the protein mutations that expose memorization. Ian explains how Leash’s measured chemical landscapes can become a sandbox for reasoning agents, with rapid experimental feedback and thousands of medicinal chemistry campaigns. We also examine the limits of DELs, moving hits toward medicines, the economics of AI drug discovery, and the experimental bottlenecks that still need solving.

We discuss:
• How DNA-encoded libraries use barcodes and sequencing to screen millions of molecules
• Catching DNA-binding artifacts with multiple barcodes per molecule
• Why Leash prioritizes reproducible measurements across many protein targets
• The BELKA Kaggle competition: four billion measurements, around 2,000 teams, and no better than chance on an unseen chemical library
• Clever Hans in ChEMBL: learning who made a molecule instead of the chemistry
• Hermes, simple baselines, careful data splits, and comparisons with Boltz
• Activity cliffs, engineered protein mutations, and models that memorize protein “nicknames”
• Agents reasoning about structure–activity relationships in plain English
• More than 10,000 medicinal chemistry campaigns in a weekend
• Going from DEL hits to mouse PK/PD, and the case for pills on difficult targets
• The Kosuri paradox: if you can collect the data, why do you need the model?
• Experimental know-how, detecting misfolded proteins, and scaling purification

—

videos.title: Robots That Predict the Future: Dyna-2 & Physical AI — Jason Ma, Dyna Robotics
videos.description:
From training a world-action model on over one million hours of human video to deploying robots that fold thousands of napkins daily at Din Tai Fung, Dyna Robotics is pushing physical AI beyond impressive demos and into real-world production. In this episode, Dyna Robotics co-founder and Chief Scientist Jason Ma joins swyx on-site to unpack how robots can learn new tasks from as little as 45 minutes of demonstrations, why predicting the future of the physical world may be the key to general-purpose robotics, and what it actually takes to build robots that work reliably for real customers.

We go deep on Dyna-2, Dyna's million-hour world-action model that combines future video prediction with robot actions, the scaling laws behind human-to-robot transfer, diffusion transformers and flow matching, and why synthetic environments and self-generated training data could unlock the next wave of robotics progress. Jason also explains why Dyna builds its own hardware instead of relying on off-the-shelf humanoids, how agentic harnesses enable robots to execute hour-long workflows, why dexterous hands and missing sensory data remain major bottlenecks, and what separates real commercial deployments from the graveyard of robotics startups. We also cover world-action models versus vision-language-action models, GPT-6 and coding agents in robotics, and Jason's journey from AlphaGo and Penn to NVIDIA, Google DeepMind, and founding Dyna.

We discuss:
- Why Dyna-2 was trained on over one million hours of human video
- World-action models: predicting future video to guide physical robot actions
- Diffusion transformers, flow matching, and real-time robotic control
- How robots learn new tasks with as little as 45 minutes of demonstrations
- Why robotics has no equivalent of the internet and data remains its biggest scaling challenge
- Human egocentric video, robot demonstrations, and cross-embodiment transfer
- Synthetic environments, simulation, and models that generate their own training data
- Why robots need on-device inference, model distillation, and custom hardware
- Why Dyna chose wheeled semi-humanoids instead of traditional bipedal robots
- The hardware bottleneck: why dexterous robot hands still overheat
- Best Western, Din Tai Fung, and the difference between robotics pilots and scaled deployments
- The Bitter Lesson of Robotics: scaling data instead of engineering specialized solutions
- Agentic harnesses and robots executing multi-step, hour-long physical workflows
- GPT-6, coding agents, and AI-generated simulation environments for robotics research
- World-action models versus VLAs, and why vision alone may not be enough
- Jason's journey through AlphaGo, Penn, NVIDIA, Google DeepMind, and the Eureka project
- Dyna's research culture, deployment-first philosophy, and vision for millions of robots

videos.title: How to kill your SaaS: what we learned replacing a $43K/yr tool with AI agents
videos.description:
A SaaS vendor quoted us $43,000 a year to run speakers for my @AIdotEngineer conferences. That would be fine if it delivered the qualitySo we asked builders to clone it with coding agents, open source, eval by the people who'd actually use it: our human events team.

72 teams submitted. This is what we learned: how the best builders split work between Claude Code and Codex, why our own AI judge ranked the winner 19th, the three things almost every clone got wrong, and why owning software is a different job from building it.

Winners 
🥇 $10,000: Valentin De Matos, OpenRostrum: https://openrostrum.com · https://github.com/openrostrum/openrostrum 
🥈 $5,000: Yazin, Conferencer: https://conferencer.cc · https://github.com/yazinsai/conferencer
